title: Scholarship
text:
If you want to study the complexity of a topological space, you might study the algebraic invariants of this space. Often, however, topological spaces such as manifolds come equipped with some geometric structure as well. How does this algebraic topological complexity translate into geometric complexity? This broad question motivates the field of so-called “quantitative topology”.
For example, if you have a nullhomotopic map (a priori, algebraic information) into your space, what is the most efficient way to perform this nullhomotopy (geometric information)? My advisor Fedya Manin has asked (and answered) similar questions in the context of simpy connected target spaces, and some of my current work is an extension of this to nilpotent targets.
I have also studied elliptic manifolds, where I asked “Given a nilpotent Lie group \(G\), what algebraic information is necessary/sufficient to guarantee that a closed manifold \(M\) is \(G\)-elliptic?” In some sense, this asks which manifolds \(M\) can be efficiently wrapped using the group \(G\) as your wrapping paper. Recent advances in related areas have opened up some clear paths forward in this investigation, where it seems likely that the Heisenberg group is a poor choice of wrapping paper for a flat torus.



I also study tiling spaces, where I am interested in extending some existing theory to the relevant nilpotent setting. For example, I extend work about the topology of Euclidean tiling spaces to tiling spaces of certain nilpotent Lie groups.

text:
About Me

A Brief Bio
The Christian liberal arts have been a driving force throughout my life. My early education at Veritas School in Newberg, Oregon developed in my a passion for lifelong learning, which led me to study Mathematics and Computer Science at Westmont College. I graduated in 2019, and—inspired by a summer of research with Dr. Russell Howell—pursued a Ph.D. in Mathematics at UC Santa Barbara. Under the direction of my advisor, Dr. Fedya Manin, I studied how nilpotent algebraic structures influence both the geometric behavior of topological spaces, as well as the patterns of aperiodic tilings. I defended my thesis in 2025. That same fall, I returned with enthusiasm to Westmont College as an Assistant Professor of Mathematics. In my leisure time, I can be found singing, reading, swimming, biking, running, (or all three), baking, and enjoying the company of my church family.

My advisor Fedya Manin has asked (and answered) similar questions in the context of simpy connected target spaces, and some of my current work is an extension of this to nilpotent targets.
I have also studied elliptic manifolds, where I asked “Given a nilpotent Lie group \(G\), what algebraic information is necessary/sufficient to guarantee that a closed manifold \(M\) is \(G\)-elliptic?” In some sense, this asks which manifolds \(M\) can be efficiently wrapped using the group \(G\) as your wrapping paper. title: Policies
text:
God called us to co-create with Him as a part of our role in bearing His image. Collaboration—in which multiple people labor side-by-side towards a common goal—is a part of God’s good design for community and relationship. Learning communities function best when students have academic integrity. Cheating is primarily an offense against your classmates because it undermines our learning community. Therefore, dishonesty of any kind may result in loss of credit for the work involved and the filing of a report with the Provost’s Office. Major or repeated infractions may result in dismissal from the course with a grade of “F”. Be familiar with the College’s plagiarism policy, found at https://www.westmont.edu/office-provost/academic-program/academic-integrity-policy.
In particular, providing someone with an electronic copy of your work is a breach of the academic integrity policy. Do not email, post online, or otherwise disseminate any of the work that you do in this class. If you keep your work on a repository, make sure it is private. In general, you may work with your peers on assignments, but make sure that you write or type up your own answers yourself. You are on your honor that the work you hand in represents your own understanding.





Westmont’s academic integrity policy prohibits us from “present[ing] another’s work as our own.” Generative AI tools such as ChatGPT attempt to do the work of writing, making, and other creative activities for their users. Therefore, students should not substitute AI-generated content or ideas for original academic work. Westmont faculty members design courses and assignments for students’ incremental and active learning through methods such as reading, summarizing, discussion, and an authentic generative process in which a student does the work of critical thinking, making meaning, and constructing messages and other creative works. I reserve the right to prohibit or limit AI use in particular assignments or for an entire course.



Math courses will build your character by asking you to persevere through challenging problems. Such character is often built through practice. Any use of LLMs (etc.) that negate this practice will end up robbing you of your education. Moreover, you will naturally perform more poorly in this course as a result. Any unapproved use of LLMs (etc.) will constitute a breach of academic integrity.



Students are advised to document their process of completing each assignment: e.g., their brainstorming, conversations, research queries, reading notes, writing or other creative expression, and the particular resources and tools used to achieve this work. Since software capabilities and AI integrations are rapidly changing, using even such tools as Grammarly without an instructor’s permission puts a student’s academic integrity at risk. When this use has been permitted, the content generated or modified by AI must be properly attributed (e.g., sharing the AI Archives link to that chat). Upon instructor request, a student should be able to narrate the process of assignment completion from start to finish, which shows how a student is learning within and across assignments.

title: Policies
Policies
text:
Assignments and Assessments

Formatting
Unless otherwise specified, all work should be handwritten (i.e., not typed up). Digital submissions will not be accepted except in rare, prearranged circumstances.


Credits & Collaborators
You may work with others on your assignments unless otherwise specified, but make sure that you write or type up your own answers yourself. You are on your honor that the work you hand in represents your own understanding. To maintain academic integrity, your work should list all people and resources you consulted while writing up your work.


Due Dates
All assignments and assessments must be turned in by the start of class on the day they are due. Work missed or turned in late (including tests) without a valid excuse will receive a zero, unless otherwise stated on the syllabus.

title: Policies
text:
Classroom Etiquette

Punctual Attendance
One of the primary resources you have in this class is the class time itself. If you miss a significant number of classes, you will almost definitely do poorly in this class. If you miss more than two weeks’ worth of classes without a valid excuse, I reserve the right to terminate you from the course with a failing grade.
Please be prepared to learn before the official start of class. Arriving late, or arriving without time to prepare yourself for class, distracts both myself and your peers. If such disruption becomes a habit, we will discuss practical methods of ensuring that class starts after you are prepared to begin. Arriving late to class constitutes a half day’s absence.


Entertainment Media
In his book “Amusing Ourselves to Death: Politics in the Age of Showbusiness” Neil Postman argues that technology whose primary vernacular is audio-visual will always present its content as “entertainment”. That is, television (and the screen-oriented media that permeate our modern era) naturally present objects as something whose purpose is amusement, rather than something worth investing thoughtful, patient, and prolonged engagement of one’s mind.
Mathematics is not amusing, nor should it be treated as such.
Starting from 5 minutes prior to class, until the end of the class period, I do not permit audio-visual media to be used in the classroom. Such media include (but are not limited to): cell phones, laptops, and tablets. For example, if class runs from 10:15-11:20am, cell phones may not be used between 10:10-11:20am while inside the classroom. This policy applies to myself. This policy may be adjusted in exceptional circumstances.

title: \(\LaTeX\) Workshop
text:
aligned environments
Sometimes a string of equalities is too long to fit on a single line, or can be made more clear by splitting it across multiple lines with justifications. Consider the following proof for instance that \(1 > 0\):

Proof. Start by letting \(x > 0\) be arbitrary. Then \(\frac{1}{x} > 0\) so that \[\begin{align*}
  1 & = x \cdot \frac{1}{x} \\
    & > 0 \cdot \frac{1}{x} \tag{since $x > 0$} \\
    & > 0 \cdot 0 \tag{since $\frac{1}{x} > 0$} \\
    & = 0.
\end{align*}\]

title: \(\LaTeX\) Workshop
text:
aligned environments cont.
\begin{align*}
  1 & = x \cdot \frac{1}{x} \\
    & > 0 \cdot \frac{1}{x} \tag{since $x > 0$} \\
    & > 0 \cdot 0 \tag{since $\frac{1}{x} > 0$} \\
    & = 0. 
\end{align*}

the & goes directly before the symbol to be aligned
the \\ indicates we are jumping to a new line
the \tag{<words>} adds a text bubble justification to the side
the code itself need not be indented—but it sure does look nicer when it is (and is soooo much easier to fix)

some subtleties

definitions, theorems, and remarks all have somewhat standard “styles”

\theoremstyle{definition}
\newtheorem{definition}{Definition}

automatically, the document keeps adding \(1\) to each theorem, and \(1\) to each definition separately. This is fine, but can be confusing (will Theorem 4 come before or after Definition 7?)

Numbering can be done using just the amsthm package. You can

give numbers that indicate what section it’s in
give a single counter that counts up for all environments

Now Theorem 6 will be followed by something 7.
But Theorem 6 likely isn’t the “6th theorem”

title: Scholarship
text:
If you want to study the complexity of a topological space, you might study the algebraic invariants of this space. Often, however, topological spaces such as manifolds come equipped with some geometric structure as well. How does this algebraic topological complexity translate into geometric complexity? This broad question motivates the field of so-called “quantitative topology”.
For example, if you have a nullhomotopic map (a priori, algebraic information) into your space, what is the most efficient way to perform this nullhomotopy (geometric information)? My advisor Fedya Manin has asked (and answered) similar questions in the context of simpy connected target spaces, and some of my current work is an extension of this to nilpotent targets.
I have also studied elliptic manifolds, where I asked “Given a nilpotent Lie group \(G\), what algebraic information is necessary/sufficient to guarantee that a closed manifold \(M\) is \(G\)-elliptic?” In some sense, this asks which manifolds \(M\) can be efficiently wrapped using the group \(G\) as your wrapping paper. Recent advances in related areas have opened up some clear paths forward in this investigation, where it seems likely that the Heisenberg group is a poor choice of wrapping paper for a flat torus.



I also study tiling spaces, where I am interested in extending some existing theory to the relevant nilpotent setting. For example, I extend work about the topology of Euclidean tiling spaces to tiling spaces of certain nilpotent Lie groups.

This broad question motivates the field of so-called “quantitative topology”.
For example, if you have a nullhomotopic map (a priori, algebraic information) into your space, what is the most efficient way to perform this nullhomotopy (geometric information)? My advisor Fedya Manin has asked (and answered) similar questions in the context of simpy connected target spaces, and some of my current work is an extension of this to nilpotent targets.
I have also studied elliptic manifolds, where I asked “Given a nilpotent Lie group \(G\), what algebraic information is necessary/sufficient to guarantee that a closed manifold \(M\) is \(G\)-elliptic?” In some sense, this asks which manifolds \(M\) can be efficiently wrapped using the group \(G\) as your wrapping paper. Recent advances in related areas have opened up some clear paths forward in this investigation, where it seems likely that the Heisenberg group is a poor choice of wrapping paper for a flat torus.



I also study tiling spaces, where I am interested in extending some existing theory to the relevant nilpotent setting. For example, I extend work about the topology of Euclidean tiling spaces to tiling spaces of certain nilpotent Lie groups.
